notation: Formulas are HTML with Unicode symbols. ν kinematic viscosity, ν_t eddy viscosity, k turbulent kinetic energy, ω specific dissipation, ε dissipation, y⁺ = u_τ y / ν, u_τ = √(τ_w/ρ).

turbulence.k_omega_sst.title: k-ω SST (Menter)
turbulence.k_omega_sst.summary: Two-equation RANS model that uses k-ω near walls and k-ε in the free stream, with a shear-stress limiter that predicts adverse-pressure-gradient separation better than either alone.
turbulence.k_omega_sst.yplus: y⁺ ≈ 1 resolves the viscous sublayer (best accuracy). OpenFOAM's ω wall function also blends to the log law for 30 < y⁺ < 300; avoid the buffer layer (5 < y⁺ < 30).
turbulence.k_omega_sst.available: OpenFOAM (default RANS model). The native solver substitutes standard k-ε.

formulation.label: Eddy viscosity
formulation.html: ν<sub>t</sub> = a<sub>1</sub>k / max(a<sub>1</sub>ω, S F<sub>2</sub>),   a<sub>1</sub> = 0.31

formulation.label: k equation
formulation.html: ∂k/∂t + U·∇k = P̃<sub>k</sub> − β*kω + ∇·[(ν + σ<sub>k</sub>ν<sub>t</sub>)∇k],   P̃<sub>k</sub> = min(P<sub>k</sub>, 10β*kω)

formulation.label: ω equation
formulation.html: ∂ω/∂t + U·∇ω = αS² − βω² + ∇·[(ν + σ<sub>ω</sub>ν<sub>t</sub>)∇ω] + 2(1 − F<sub>1</sub>)σ<sub>ω2</sub>(1/ω)∇k·∇ω

formulation.label: Constants
formulation.html: β* = 0.09; F<sub>1</sub> blends the k-ω (inner) and k-ε (outer) coefficient sets

use_cases: External aerodynamics with separation (vehicles, brackets, bluff bodies)
Adverse pressure gradients, diffusers, turbomachinery
General-purpose default when unsure
pitfalls: Stagnation regions still over-produce k slightly; the production limiter keeps it bounded.
Inlet ω sets the free-stream turbulence decay: a too-small length scale makes inlet turbulence vanish before the body.
Steady RANS of a bluff body has an unsteady wake: judge convergence on forces, not only residuals.
references: F. R. Menter, “Two-equation eddy-viscosity turbulence models for engineering applications,” AIAA Journal 32(8):1598–1605, 1994.
F. R. Menter, M. Kuntz, R. Langtry, “Ten years of industrial experience with the SST turbulence model,” Turbulence, Heat and Mass Transfer 4, 2003.
D. C. Wilcox, Turbulence Modeling for CFD, 3rd ed., DCW Industries, 2006.

turbulence.k_epsilon.title: Standard k-ε
turbulence.k_epsilon.summary: Robust two-equation RANS model for fully turbulent flows away from walls, used with wall functions; it tends to under-predict separation under adverse pressure gradients.
turbulence.k_epsilon.yplus: Wall functions: 30 < y⁺ < 300. Do not resolve to y⁺ ≈ 1 with the standard model: it has no low-Re damping.

formulation.label: Eddy viscosity
formulation.html: ν<sub>t</sub> = C<sub>μ</sub> k² / ε

formulation.label: k equation
formulation.html: ∂k/∂t + U·∇k = P<sub>k</sub> − ε + ∇·[(ν + ν<sub>t</sub>/σ<sub>k</sub>)∇k]

formulation.label: ε equation
formulation.html: ∂ε/∂t + U·∇ε = C<sub>1ε</sub>(ε/k)P<sub>k</sub> − C<sub>2ε</sub>ε²/k + ∇·[(ν + ν<sub>t</sub>/σ<sub>ε</sub>)∇ε]

formulation.label: Constants
formulation.html: C<sub>μ</sub> = 0.09, C<sub>1ε</sub> = 1.44, C<sub>2ε</sub> = 1.92, σ<sub>k</sub> = 1.0, σ<sub>ε</sub> = 1.3

use_cases: Internal ducts and pipes, mixing, free shear layers
Quick industrial estimates with coarse near-wall meshes
pitfalls: Delays or misses separation under adverse pressure gradients.
Stagnation-point anomaly: excessive k on the front of bluff bodies.
Cells in the viscous sublayer (y⁺ < 11) make standard wall functions inaccurate.
references: B. E. Launder, D. B. Spalding, “The numerical computation of turbulent flows,” Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 3(2):269–289, 1974.
S. B. Pope, Turbulent Flows, Cambridge University Press, 2000, ch. 10.

turbulence.spalart_allmaras.title: Spalart–Allmaras
turbulence.spalart_allmaras.summary: One-equation RANS model for a modified eddy viscosity ν̃, calibrated for aerodynamic boundary layers; cheap and robust for attached wall-bounded flows.
turbulence.spalart_allmaras.yplus: Designed for y⁺ ≈ 1. Paramfabric pairs it with Spalding's wall law (nutUSpaldingWallFunction), which tolerates y⁺ up to ~100.

formulation.label: Eddy viscosity
formulation.html: ν<sub>t</sub> = ν̃ f<sub>v1</sub>,   f<sub>v1</sub> = χ³/(χ³ + c<sub>v1</sub>³),   χ = ν̃/ν,   c<sub>v1</sub> = 7.1

formulation.label: ν̃ equation
formulation.html: Dν̃/Dt = c<sub>b1</sub>S̃ν̃ − c<sub>w1</sub>f<sub>w</sub>(ν̃/d)² + (1/σ)[∇·((ν + ν̃)∇ν̃) + c<sub>b2</sub>|∇ν̃|²]

formulation.label: Inlet
formulation.html: ν̃ = 3ν to 5ν for a fully turbulent inflow (Paramfabric uses 3ν)

use_cases: Wings, airfoils, fuselages: attached or mildly separated aerodynamic flows
Large meshes where one transport equation saves cost
pitfalls: Poor for free shear flows (jets, wakes far downstream) and massive separation.
No k field: turbulence intensity cannot be post-processed.
Needs wall distance d everywhere; very thin gaps can distort it.
references: P. R. Spalart, S. R. Allmaras, “A one-equation turbulence model for aerodynamic flows,” AIAA Paper 92-0439, 1992; La Recherche Aérospatiale 1:5–21, 1994.

turbulence.laminar.title: Laminar (no turbulence model)
turbulence.laminar.summary: Solves the steady incompressible Navier–Stokes equations directly, which is valid only below transition (pipe Re_D < 2300, flat plate Re_x < 5×10⁵).
turbulence.laminar.yplus: Not applicable: resolve the boundary layer with at least ~10 cells across its thickness δ ≈ 5x/√Re_x.
turbulence.laminar.available: OpenFOAM and the native solver. Automatic mode selects it below Re = 2000.

formulation.label: Momentum
formulation.html: (U·∇)U = −∇p/ρ + ν∇²U

use_cases: Microfluidics, slow viscous flows, low-speed internal flows
Verification against analytic solutions (Poiseuille, Couette)
pitfalls: At high Re a steady laminar solution of a separated flow does not exist; SIMPLE will oscillate or diverge.
Transitional flows are neither laminar nor fully turbulent; both choices carry model error.
references: F. M. White, Viscous Fluid Flow, 3rd ed., McGraw-Hill, 2006.

mesh.tetrahedral.title: Tetrahedral mesh
mesh.tetrahedral.summary: Fully automatic body-fitted mesh for any CAD shape; use quadratic Tet10 for structures and prism inflation layers for CFD walls.
mesh.tetrahedral.yplus: Tetrahedra alone resolve near-wall gradients poorly. Add prism inflation layers sized for the turbulence model's y⁺ target.

formulation.label: Quality (radius ratio)
formulation.html: q = 3 r<sub>in</sub>/R<sub>circ</sub> ∈ (0, 1], equilateral = 1; Paramfabric grades meshes on min and mean q

formulation.label: Linear tet strain
formulation.html: Tet4 has constant strain per element: bending needs many elements, while Tet10 (quadratic) captures linear strain

use_cases: Complex or imported geometry
Structural FEA with Tet10
CFD with prism layers when hex meshing is impractical
pitfalls: Linear Tet4 is overly stiff in bending (locking): use the quadratic order for FEA.
In CFD tets add numerical diffusion and non-orthogonality: expect ~10–16% pressure-drop error at ~7 cells per hydraulic diameter (Paramfabric duct validation).
Needs 5–6× more cells than hexahedra for the same resolution.
references: J. R. Shewchuk, “What is a good linear finite element?”, 11th International Meshing Roundtable, 2002.
S. E. Benzley et al., “A comparison of all-hexagonal and all-tetrahedral finite element meshes for elastic and elasto-plastic analysis,” 4th International Meshing Roundtable, 1995.

mesh.hexahedral.title: Hexahedral mesh
mesh.hexahedral.summary: Fewer, better-aligned cells for the same accuracy. Paramfabric produces all-hex meshes by subdividing each tetrahedron into four hexahedra.
mesh.hexahedral.yplus: Aligned hex layers fit boundary layers naturally; subdivision hexes are not wall-aligned, so CFD in Paramfabric always uses tets + prisms.

formulation.label: Subdivision
formulation.html: 1 tet → 4 hexes (gmsh SubdivisionAlgorithm 2): all-hex, but with skewed cells near tet corners

formulation.label: Hex20
formulation.html: Serendipity quadratic hexahedron: accurate bending with 1–2 elements through the thickness

use_cases: Structural FEA where Hex20 accuracy per DOF matters
Prismatic and swept parts
pitfalls: Subdivided hexes have lower shape quality than swept or multiblock hexes.
Hex8 (linear) shows shear locking in bending: prefer Hex20.
Not available for CFD in Paramfabric.
references: S. E. Benzley et al., “A comparison of all-hexagonal and all-tetrahedral finite element meshes for elastic and elasto-plastic analysis,” 4th International Meshing Roundtable, 1995.
C. Geuzaine, J.-F. Remacle, “Gmsh: a 3-D finite element mesh generator,” IJNME 79(11):1309–1331, 2009.

engine.lbm.title: Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM)
engine.lbm.summary: Solves a discrete Boltzmann equation on a Cartesian lattice with explicit collide-and-stream steps; very fast on GPUs for transient flows, but not natively a steady-RANS method.
engine.lbm.yplus: Wall-resolved LBM at high Re needs enormous cell counts; practical LBM codes use LES with wall models (y⁺ of 30–100 or more).
engine.lbm.available: Not available in Paramfabric. Listed for comparison only.

formulation.label: Lattice BGK
formulation.html: f<sub>i</sub>(x + c<sub>i</sub>Δt, t + Δt) = f<sub>i</sub>(x, t) − (1/τ)[f<sub>i</sub> − f<sub>i</sub><sup>eq</sup>]

formulation.label: Viscosity
formulation.html: ν = c<sub>s</sub>²(τ − ½)Δt,   c<sub>s</sub> = Δx/(√3 Δt)

formulation.label: Velocity sets
formulation.html: D3Q19 / D3Q27; weakly compressible, Ma ≲ 0.1–0.3

use_cases: Transient aerodynamics and aeroacoustics
Very complex geometry without meshing (voxelized)
Pedestrian wind comfort, urban flows
pitfalls: Staircase walls unless interpolated boundary conditions are used.
Steady-state answers require long transient averaging.
Compressibility error grows with lattice Mach number.
references: T. Krüger et al., The Lattice Boltzmann Method: Principles and Practice, Springer, 2017.
S. Chen, G. D. Doolen, “Lattice Boltzmann method for fluid flows,” Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics 30:329–364, 1998.

engine.fvm_navier_stokes.title: Finite-volume Navier–Stokes (FVM)
engine.fvm_navier_stokes.summary: Integrates conservation laws over body-fitted control volumes with implicit pressure–velocity coupling (SIMPLE); the industry standard for steady RANS. Paramfabric runs it with OpenFOAM simpleFoam.
engine.fvm_navier_stokes.yplus: Set by the turbulence model: ≈1 for SST/SA resolved, 30–300 with wall functions.
engine.fvm_navier_stokes.available: OpenFOAM simpleFoam (production) and the native experimental solver.

formulation.label: Conservation
formulation.html: ∮<sub>∂V</sub> (UU − ν<sub>eff</sub>∇U)·dS = −∮<sub>∂V</sub> p dS,   ∮<sub>∂V</sub> U·dS = 0

formulation.label: SIMPLE(C)
formulation.html: predict U* from momentum → solve ∇·(1/a<sub>P</sub>∇p′) = ∇·U* → correct p, U; under-relax α<sub>U</sub>, α<sub>p</sub>

use_cases: Steady RANS for drag, lift, and pressure drop
Body-fitted meshes with boundary-layer prisms
Internal and external incompressible flow
pitfalls: Mesh non-orthogonality and skewness degrade accuracy; check checkMesh output.
Residuals can plateau for physically unsteady flows; monitor integrated forces.
references: S. V. Patankar, Numerical Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Hemisphere, 1980.
J. H. Ferziger, M. Perić, Computational Methods for Fluid Dynamics, 3rd ed., Springer, 2002.
H. G. Weller et al., “A tensorial approach to computational continuum mechanics using object-oriented techniques,” Computers in Physics 12(6):620–631, 1998.

bc.velocity_inlet.title: Velocity inlet
bc.velocity_inlet.summary: Prescribes the incoming velocity (Dirichlet) with zero-gradient pressure; turbulence enters as intensity and length scale.

formulation.label: Velocity
formulation.html: U = U<sub>in</sub> (external box), or |U| normal to the face (internal inlet)

formulation.label: Turbulence
formulation.html: k = 3/2 (I U)²,   ω = √k / (C<sub>μ</sub><sup>1/4</sup> ℓ),   ε = C<sub>μ</sub><sup>3/4</sup> k<sup>3/2</sup>/ℓ

use_cases: Wind-tunnel inflow for external flow
Duct and pipe inlets with known flow rate
pitfalls: Too close to the body (less than 3–5 lengths upstream) distorts the approach flow.
Do not also prescribe velocity at the outlet: the problem becomes over-constrained.
references: H. K. Versteeg, W. Malalasekera, An Introduction to Computational Fluid Dynamics, 2nd ed., Pearson, 2007, ch. 9.

bc.pressure_outlet.title: Pressure outlet
bc.pressure_outlet.summary: Fixes the static (gauge) pressure and lets velocity leave freely; backflow is blocked (inletOutlet).

formulation.label: Pressure
formulation.html: p = 0 (gauge; OpenFOAM's p is kinematic, p/ρ)

formulation.label: Velocity
formulation.html: ∂U/∂n = 0 for outflow; U = 0 for inflow (inletOutlet)

use_cases: Exit of external domains and ducts
pitfalls: An outlet cutting through a recirculation zone causes backflow and unstable convergence: place it 5–10 body lengths downstream.
Gauge pressure only: add the ambient pressure for absolute values.
references: H. K. Versteeg, W. Malalasekera, An Introduction to Computational Fluid Dynamics, 2nd ed., Pearson, 2007, ch. 9.

bc.no_slip_wall.title: No-slip wall
bc.no_slip_wall.summary: Fluid velocity equals the wall velocity (zero here); turbulence walls use the model's wall treatment.
bc.no_slip_wall.yplus: Choose the first-cell height for the model: y⁺ ≈ 1 (SST, SA resolved) or 30–300 (wall functions). The inflation-layer tool computes it from a target y⁺.

formulation.label: First cell
formulation.html: y<sub>1</sub> = y⁺ν/u<sub>τ</sub>,   u<sub>τ</sub> = U√(C<sub>f</sub>/2),   C<sub>f</sub> ≈ 0.058 Re<sup>−0.2</sup> (turbulent) or 1.328/√Re (laminar)

formulation.label: Wall functions
formulation.html: kqRWallFunction, omegaWallFunction / epsilonWallFunction, nutkWallFunction (SA: nutUSpaldingWallFunction)

use_cases: Every solid surface in contact with the fluid
pitfalls: A first cell in the buffer layer (5 < y⁺ < 30) degrades wall shear and drag for all models.
references: D. B. Spalding, “A single formula for the law of the wall,” Journal of Applied Mechanics 28(3):455–458, 1961.

bc.symmetry.title: Symmetry / slip
bc.symmetry.summary: Zero normal velocity and zero normal gradients: a frictionless plane. Paramfabric applies it to the far-field sides of the flow box.
use_cases: Far-field sides of external domains
Half models of symmetric geometry and symmetric flow
pitfalls: Only valid if the flow really is symmetric: wakes that shed alternately are not.
Keep blockage (body frontal area / box cross-section) below about 5% or the sides accelerate the flow.
references: J. H. Ferziger, M. Perić, Computational Methods for Fluid Dynamics, 3rd ed., Springer, 2002, §8.10.

mesh.inflation.title: Prism inflation layers
mesh.inflation.summary: Thin prism layers grown from the walls resolve the boundary layer with high-aspect-ratio cells aligned with the wall.
mesh.inflation.yplus: The first height comes from the target y⁺ (flat-plate skin friction estimate). Check the y⁺ reported after the solve and adjust.

formulation.label: Layer heights
formulation.html: h<sub>i</sub> = h<sub>1</sub> g<sup>i−1</sup>,   total = h<sub>1</sub>(gⁿ − 1)/(g − 1)

formulation.label: First height
formulation.html: h<sub>1</sub> = y⁺ν/u<sub>τ</sub>, capped so the stack stays below 20% of the local cell size

use_cases: Every turbulent CFD case with drag, lift, or heat transfer at walls
pitfalls: Growth ratios above ~1.3 produce a jump to the tetrahedra above the stack.
Very sharp concave corners can make extrusion fail; Paramfabric then meshes without layers and logs it.
references: C. Geuzaine, J.-F. Remacle, “Gmsh: a 3-D finite element mesh generator,” IJNME 79(11):1309–1331, 2009.

solver.relaxation.title: Under-relaxation factors α_U, α_p
solver.relaxation.summary: Fractions of each SIMPLE update that are kept; lower values stabilize difficult cases at the cost of more iterations.

formulation.label: Update
formulation.html: φ<sup>new</sup> = φ<sup>old</sup> + α(φ* − φ<sup>old</sup>)

formulation.label: Defaults
formulation.html: SIMPLEC (consistent): α<sub>U</sub> = 0.9, α<sub>turb</sub> = 0.7, no pressure relaxation. Classic SIMPLE: α<sub>U</sub> + α<sub>p</sub> ≈ 1 (e.g. 0.7 / 0.3).

use_cases: Diverging or oscillating runs: lower α_U to 0.5–0.7 and set α_p = 0.3
pitfalls: Relaxation changes the path, not the converged answer; very low values only slow convergence.
references: S. V. Patankar, Numerical Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Hemisphere, 1980, §6.7.

solver.tolerance.title: Convergence and matrix tolerances
solver.tolerance.summary: The residual target ends the run; linear-solver tolerances control how accurately each inner matrix system is solved.

formulation.label: Residual control
formulation.html: stop when every initial residual < target (default 10⁻⁵), or when Cd is steady within ±0.5% over the last 20% of iterations

formulation.label: Linear solvers
formulation.html: GAMG for p (tolerance 10⁻⁷, relTol 0.05), smoothSolver for U and turbulence (10⁻⁸, relTol 0.1)

use_cases: Tighten for accurate integrated forces; loosen for quick trend studies
pitfalls: Residual targets below the plateau of a physically unsteady flow are never reached.
references: OpenFOAM v2506 User Guide, “Solution and algorithm control.”

structural.beam.title: 1D beam (frame) element
structural.beam.summary: Models a slender member by its axis line and cross-section (A, Iy, Iz, J): six DOF per node, exact for end-loaded Euler–Bernoulli beams.

formulation.label: Bending
formulation.html: EI w′′′′ = q,   tip deflection PL³/(3EI) for a cantilever

formulation.label: Stress
formulation.html: σ = |N|/A + |M<sub>y</sub>|c<sub>z</sub>/I<sub>y</sub> + |M<sub>z</sub>|c<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>z</sub>

formulation.label: I-section
formulation.html: I<sub>y</sub> = [b h³ − (b − t<sub>w</sub>)(h − 2t<sub>f</sub>)³]/12

use_cases: Frames, trusses, stiffeners, shafts: length ≫ section depth (L/h > 10)
pitfalls: Shear deformation is neglected (short, deep beams are too stiff).
No local buckling or stress concentrations at joints.
references: W. Weaver, J. M. Gere, Matrix Analysis of Framed Structures, 3rd ed., Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1990.

structural.shell.title: 2D shell element
structural.shell.summary: Models thin walls by their surface and thickness: CST membrane plus DKT plate bending per flat triangle, optionally with the mid-surface offset from the selected face.

formulation.label: Offset
formulation.html: u<sub>mid</sub> = u + θ × (e n): a rigid link to the face, so offset shells and beams act compositely

formulation.label: Check
formulation.html: simply supported square plate: w<sub>max</sub> = 0.00406 q a⁴/D (Paramfabric: −0.1% at 24×24)

use_cases: Sheet metal, panels, thin-walled housings: thickness ≪ span (t/L < 1/20)
pitfalls: Kirchhoff theory: thick plates (t/L > 1/10) are too stiff.
Flat facets approximate curvature: refine curved faces.
references: J.-L. Batoz, K.-J. Bathe, L.-W. Ho, “A study of three-node triangular plate bending elements,” IJNME 15(12):1771–1812, 1980.

view.cut_plane.title: Cutting plane
view.cut_plane.summary: Slices the volume mesh in the browser to show interior cells, contours, and velocity vectors on any X, Y, or Z plane.

formulation.label: Section
formulation.html: marching tetrahedra: field values interpolated linearly along cut edges, φ = φ<sub>a</sub> + (φ<sub>b</sub> − φ<sub>a</sub>) d<sub>a</sub>/(d<sub>a</sub> − d<sub>b</sub>)

use_cases: Inspect wakes, recirculation, interior stress
pitfalls: Shown on the undeformed mesh for FEA; meshes above 600k tetrahedra are not sent to the browser (use the VTK file).

view.iso_surface.title: Iso-surface
view.iso_surface.summary: Extracts the surface where a volume field equals a chosen level (e.g. T = 310 K or |U| = 0.5 m/s) in the browser and colors it by the legend field. Inlet-seeded streamlines are traced in the browser too when the solver did not provide any.

formulation.label: Iso-surface
formulation.html: marching tetrahedra on d = φ − φ<sub>iso</sub>: one triangle per 1|3 sign split, a quad (a,c)(a,d)(b,d)(b,c) per 2|2 split

formulation.label: Streamlines
formulation.html: midpoint RK2, x<sub>n+1</sub> = x<sub>n</sub> + Δt·U(x<sub>n</sub> + ½Δt·U(x<sub>n</sub>)), Δt = Δs/|U|, U interpolated barycentrically per tetrahedron

use_cases: Thermal plumes and hot spots in CHT
Low-speed recirculation pockets (|U| iso)
Pressure lobes around bluff bodies
pitfalls: Piecewise-linear: the surface is only as smooth as the mesh.
Streamlines stop at walls, zero-velocity points and the domain edge; particle animation shows transit time, not a transient solution.
references: A. Doi, A. Koide, “An efficient method of triangulating equi-valued surfaces by using tetrahedral cells,” IEICE Trans. E74(1):214–224, 1991.

structural.modal.title: Modal analysis
structural.modal.summary: Natural frequencies f_n and mode shapes of the supported structure (solid, or the assigned beams and shells). Loads are ignored; only supports, stiffness and mass matter.

formulation.label: Eigenproblem
formulation.html: K φ = ω² M φ, f = ω / 2π; consistent mass M = ∫ ρ Nᵀ N dV

formulation.label: Solver
formulation.html: shift-invert Lanczos (ARPACK) with a small negative shift σ so rigid-body modes of an under-supported model stay solvable

formulation.label: Effective mass
formulation.html: m<sub>eff,i</sub> = (φ<sub>i</sub>ᵀ M r)² / (φ<sub>i</sub>ᵀ M φ<sub>i</sub>), reported as a fraction of the total mass along x, y, z

use_cases: Check resonance against excitation (motors, fans, road input)
Seismic/shock mode selection: include modes until Σ m_eff ≥ 90 %
pitfalls: Mode shapes are normalized (unit max |φ|): their amplitude has no physical meaning.
Unsupported models have zero-frequency rigid-body modes.
Tet4 meshes are too stiff: frequencies converge from above, so use second order.
references: K.-J. Bathe, Finite Element Procedures, 2nd ed., ch. 10–11, 2014.
R. D. Blevins, Formulas for Natural Frequency and Mode Shape, 1979.

physics.cht.title: Conjugate heat transfer
physics.cht.summary: Couples conduction in the solid bodies with convection in the coolant around them (OpenFOAM chtMultiRegionSimpleFoam). A heater face injects a total power; the coolant carries it out of the outlet.

formulation.label: Solid
formulation.html: ∇·(κ<sub>s</sub> ∇T) = 0 (heSolidThermo, constant κ)

formulation.label: Fluid
formulation.html: steady laminar Navier–Stokes + energy in enthalpy h, constant ρ (heRhoThermo, rhoConst)

formulation.label: Interface
formulation.html: compressible::turbulentTemperatureCoupledBaffleMixed: T<sub>f</sub> = T<sub>s</sub>, κ<sub>f</sub> ∂T<sub>f</sub>/∂n = κ<sub>s</sub> ∂T<sub>s</sub>/∂n on conforming mappedWall patches

formulation.label: Check
formulation.html: energy balance ṁ c<sub>p</sub> (T̄<sub>out</sub> − T<sub>in</sub>) = Q, thermal resistance R = (T<sub>s,max</sub> − T<sub>in</sub>) / Q

use_cases: Cold plates, heat sinks, liquid-cooled housings
pitfalls: Laminar only: check Re = U D / ν < ~2000 in the channel.
The peak solid temperature is mesh-sensitive at coarse sizes; refine at the interface until it stops changing.
The energy-balance check is the convergence criterion: residuals alone are not enough.
references: OpenFOAM v2506 tutorials: heatTransfer/chtMultiRegionSimpleFoam.
F. P. Incropera et al., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed., 2011.

Generation time: Seconds, fully automatic for any B-Rep
Fast in Paramfabric (tet subdivision); swept or multiblock hex is manual and slow
Accuracy: Tet10: excellent for FEA. Tet4 locks in bending. CFD: more diffusion (+10–16% dp at 7 cells/D_h)
Hex20: best accuracy per DOF. Subdivision hexes are less regular than swept hexes
Cell count: 5–6× more cells for the same resolution
Boundary-layer fit: Wall-aligned layers when swept; subdivision hexes are not aligned
Cons: Hard to generate for complex parts
Recommended use: CFD (with prisms), FEA with Tet10, complex imports
FEA of blocky or swept parts with Hex20

Method: Conservation over control volumes, implicit SIMPLE
Accuracy: High for transient, resolved flows; wall treatment limits high-Re accuracy
High for steady attached and separated RANS with good near-wall meshes
Computational cost: Very fast per cell on GPUs, needs many cells and time steps
Fewer cells, more work per cell, converges to steady state
Pros: No meshing, transient physics, GPU scaling
Mature RANS, wall resolution, steady answers
Cons: Weak compressibility, staircase walls, averaging time

Accuracy: Best general RANS accuracy for wall-bounded and separating flows
Good for internal and free shear flows; weak under adverse pressure gradients
Very good for attached aerodynamic boundary layers
Exact physics below transition, invalid above
